Elms
ELMZ
n. pl. (a shade tree named among the groves of Israel's idolatry)
Old English elm, from Latin ulmus. In Hosea it renders Hebrew elah, a terebinth or strong tree — elsewhere translated oak or teil tree; the KJV varies the English because the Hebrew names a class of large shade trees rather than one species.

Biblical Definition

They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains, and burn incense upon the hills, under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good. Hosea is describing the high places, and the detail he chooses is the comfort of the shade. The trees were pleasant; that is why the worship was held there. Israel's idolatry did not feel like apostasy from the inside — it felt like a good day on a hill under a broad tree, with incense, in a place their fathers had used. That is precisely what made it so hard to root out, and why the law had ordered the groves destroyed before the people ever entered: ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree. Isaiah tells the same people they shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired, and describes them enflaming themselves with idols under every green tree and slaying their children in the valleys. The sentence Hosea passes is exact and terrible — therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom. What the fathers did comfortably under a good shadow, the daughters paid for. False worship is never contained to the generation that finds it pleasant.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a tree of the genus Ulmus, valued for its shade and timber; in Scripture, a large spreading tree of the groves.

expand to see more

ELM, n. A tree of the genus Ulmus, much valued for its shade and for the beauty of its form.

GROVE, n. A cluster of trees of no great extent; in Scripture, a wood or cluster of trees consecrated to idol worship.

HIGH-PLACE, n. In Scripture, an eminence used for the worship of idols or for sacrifice.

SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light.

INCENSE, n. Perfume exhaled by fire; the odors of spices and gums, burnt in religious rites.

Key Scripture

Hosea 4:13 — "They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains, and burn incense upon the hills, under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good: therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your spouses shall commit adultery."

Deuteronomy 12:2 — "Ye shall utterly destroy all the places, wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree:"

Isaiah 1:29 — "For they shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired, and ye shall be confounded for the gardens that ye have chosen."

Isaiah 57:5 — "Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks?"

Modern Corruption

Worship is evaluated by how it feels — the shadow being good — rather than by whether God commanded it; Hosea names the pleasantness as the very thing that kept Israel in the groves.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the pleasantness of a religious setting proves nothing about whether God is in it. Because the shadow thereof is good is Hosea's explanation for a whole nation's false worship, and it is an explanation, not an excuse. The question Scripture puts to any act of worship is the one put at Sinai and repeated by Christ against the traditions of the elders: who required this at your hand? In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

The second half of Hosea's verse is the part that should sober any father. Therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your spouses shall commit adultery. The men are in view throughout the passage; the consequence lands on the household. God says two verses later, I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, for themselves are separated with whores. A generation that worships comfortably in a place God never appointed does not pay the whole bill itself. What is treated as a harmless preference in a father becomes a settled practice in a child.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew elah (H424), a terebinth or strong tree; allon (H437), an oak; libneh (H3839), the poplar; bamah (H1116), a high place.

expand to see more

Hebrew elah (H424) — a terebinth; rendered elm here and oak or teil tree elsewhere.

Hebrew allon (H437) — an oak; the first tree in Hosea's list.

Hebrew libneh (H3839) — the poplar or white tree; the second, and the rods Jacob peeled.

Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the standing word for the hilltop shrines Judah's good kings kept failing to remove.

Hebrew asherah (H842) — a grove or wooden idol; what Deuteronomy commanded to be cut down.

Usage

"“under oaks and poplars and elms” — the furniture of the high places."

"“because the shadow thereof is good” — the reason given, and the whole problem."

"“ye shall be ashamed of the oaks which ye have desired” — Isaiah on the end of it."
